label: When it hits you
rationale: Reactions to a big moment like a concert, a sad film or big news: tears come, goosebumps rise, it hasn't sunk in yet.
mixUps: Each reaction is the subject with its own verb: namida ga deru (not naku, which is crying outright), torihada ga tatsu (stand, not deru). jikkan wakanai (it hasn't sunk in) sounds close to wakannai (I don't get it).

targets.trap: Learners use naku (cry) for any tears, but naku is crying from emotion. Watery eyes from a yawn, onions, hay fever or laughing are namida ga deru: akubi shitara namida deta. At a moving film both work: naita, or the softer namida deta (I teared up).
targets.use: Tears that come on their own, mostly past: namida deta after a yawn, onions, laughing too hard or a moving film, with ga often dropped. namida dete kita is welling up as it happens, and namida desou (I'm going to cry) comes at a moving scene; crying outright is naku.
targets.notes: namida ga tomaranai means the tears won't stop, from a sad film or from hay fever.

example.english: I laughed so hard I teared up.

examplePolite.ja: 笑いすぎて涙が出ました。
examplePolite.english: I laughed so hard I teared up.

targets.verbSense: stand, rise; here the bumps on your skin stand up
targets.trap: 'Get goosebumps' pulls learners toward morau or dekiru, but goosebumps 'stand up': torihada ga tatsu. It's the plain word for all goosebumps: cold, fear or being moved.
targets.use: Mostly past as a reaction, with ga dropped: torihada tatta! after a great song, a scary story or a cold blast of air. mite, torihada tatteru (look, I've got goosebumps) shows them as they happen.
targets.notes: Once only for cold, fear or disgust; for being moved it's now standard. torihada mono (goosebump-worthy) is the casual compliment.

example.english: That song just gave me goosebumps!

examplePolite.romaji: ima no uta, torihada ga tachimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今の歌、鳥肌が立ちました。
examplePolite.english: That song just gave me goosebumps.

targets.trap: Learners reach for mada wakaranai or rikai shite nai, which sound like you don't understand the news. Japanese says the real feeling hasn't welled up: mada jikkan wakanai. mada shinjirarenai (I still can't believe it) also works.
partners: imeeji (imeeji ga wakanai: can't picture it)
targets.use: Mostly negative, after big news like passing an exam, a new job, a wedding or a baby: mada jikkan wakanai (it hasn't sunk in yet). jikkan nai says the same, and the polite mada jikkan ga wakanai desu is a stock line in interviews. Once it does sink in: yatto jikkan waite kita.
targets.notes: Don't mix up wakanai (doesn't well up, from waku) with wakannai (don't get it): one n apart.

example.ja: まだ全然実感湧かない。
example.english: It still hasn't sunk in at all.

examplePolite.romaji: mada zenzen jikkan ga wakanai desu.
examplePolite.ja: まだ全然実感が湧かないです。
examplePolite.english: It still hasn't sunk in at all.
